narrative:
The 2020 Washington Nationals entered the pandemic-shortened season as defending World Series champions, but the magic from that October run proved impossible to recapture. After a modest 3-4 July to open the 60-game sprint, the team stumbled badly in August, going just 9-17 as their bullpen — anchored by World Series hero Daniel Hudson — became an unexpected liability. Hudson's name appeared repeatedly in the wrong column, surrendering critical home runs that swung games decisively away from Washington. The ERA ballooned to 5.09 across the roster, a number that told the story of a pitching staff unable to hold leads in a season with no margin for error.

August was the month the Nationals' playoff hopes quietly died. The bullpen's collapse was not a slow bleed but a series of sudden, devastating blows — Hudson giving up a walk-off type blast to Dansby Swanson, rookie Wil Crowe getting tagged, and the run prevention simply never coming together. While the offense showed flashes of its star power, particularly from Juan Soto and Trea Turner, the team could not outscore its pitching woes consistently enough to stay in contention in the expanded-but-still-competitive NL East.

September brought a split record of 14-14 — a .500 month that was simultaneously too little and too late, yet contained some of the season's most genuinely exciting moments. Late-season revelations like Yadiel Hernandez, a 32-year-old Cuban defector making his major league debut, provided unexpected spark. Hernandez delivered a clutch double and a home run in the final week, offering a hopeful subplot in an otherwise disappointing campaign. Youngsters like Luis García Jr. and contributions from veterans like Asdrúbal Cabrera gave glimpses of what the next Nationals core might look like.

Ultimately, a 26-34 record and a missed playoff berth marked a jarring descent from the championship summit. The 2020 Nationals were a team caught between the fading glow of a championship roster and the not-yet-ready emergence of their next generation. The bullpen, particularly Hudson's struggles, was the fatal flaw in a short season that punished every mistake twice as hard. Washington's title defense ended not with a bang but with a September muddle — flashes of brilliance bookending a summer that slipped away in the dog days of August.

chapters.title: Champions No More
chapters.description: The defending World Series champions stumble out of the gate as the bullpen immediately becomes a liability, surrendering crushing home runs in the opening weeks.

chapters.title: August Collapse
chapters.description: A brutal 9-17 August buries Washington's playoff hopes as Daniel Hudson's meltdown against Atlanta delivers the most damaging blow of the season.

chapters.title: Searching for Answers
chapters.description: The Nationals try to stop the bleeding in late August but a series of costly home runs allowed by young pitchers signals that the pitching problems run deeper than the bullpen.

chapters.title: September Flickers
chapters.description: A 14-14 September brings competitive baseball and dramatic swings, with Trea Turner's solo shot and a clutch Michael A. Taylor single against Atlanta providing rare moments of joy.

chapters.title: Next Generation Emerges
chapters.description: With the playoffs out of reach, young Nationals like Luis García Jr. and surprise debutant Yadiel Hernandez deliver the season's most triumphant moments, offering hope for the future.
